x: C is incorrect: the Prime Minister and his Council are responsible only to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)), even if he is a Rajya Sabha member. He is the real executive head, appointed by the President.
t: Collective responsibility runs to the Lok Sabha alone.

x: Both are true and R explains A: since the President is only the constitutional head, real executive power is exercised by the Prime Minister and his Council.
t: Ask whether R is why the PM holds real power.

x: Both are true: the President administers the Prime Minister's oath and receives his resignation.
t: Recall the PM's oath and resignation both involve the President.

x: All four are chaired by the Prime Minister: NITI Aayog, the National Development Council, the National Integration Council and the Inter-State Council.
t: Recall the bodies the PM heads.

x: Article 74 – Council of Ministers to aid and advise; 75 – appointment and tenure of Ministers; 78 – duties of the PM towards the President; 75(3) – collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha.
t: Match each Article to its role.

x: All four are correct: Article 75(1A), added by the 91st Amendment (2003), caps the Union ministry at 15% of the Lok Sabha's strength, and Article 164(1A) applies the same cap in the States.
t: Recall the 15% rule and where it lives.

x: Both are true and R explains A: because the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, a successful no-confidence motion forces all Ministers, including the PM, to resign.
t: Ask whether collective responsibility causes the joint resignation.

x: The Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers (Article 74). The President is the head of State, not of the Council.
t: Separate head of State from head of the Council.

x: Both are true: the Prime Minister is the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha, normally of the single majority party.
t: Recall how the PM is chosen.

x: Both are true and R explains A: a non-member can be appointed PM because Article 75(5) gives him six months to enter Parliament.
t: Check whether R makes A possible.

x: All three: as head of the Council the PM selects Ministers, allocates portfolios and can ask any Minister to resign.
t: Recall the PM's powers over his Ministers.

x: Under Article 78 the PM communicates all Council decisions, furnishes information the President asks for, submits a Minister's decision to the Council when the President so requires, and links the President and the Council.
t: Match each duty to its trigger.

x: All three are correct: the PM is the leader of the Lok Sabha, its Leader of the House, and the chief spokesperson of the government.
t: Recall the PM's roles in Parliament.

x: NITI Aayog (2015) is the PM-chaired think tank that replaced the Planning Commission; the NDMA is the PM-chaired apex body under the Disaster Management Act, 2005; and the NDC, with all Chief Ministers, approved Five-Year Plans. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Separate the former body from current ones.
s: Match List-I with List-II: List-I a. NITI Aayog b. Planning Commission c. National Disaster Management Authority d. National Development Council List-II i. Earlier planning body chaired by the Prime Minister, replaced in 2015 ii. Policy think tank chaired by the Prime Minister, set up in 2015 iii. Apex disaster body chaired by the Prime Minister under the 2005 Act iv. Body chaired by the Prime Minister, with all Chief Ministers, that approved Five-Year Plans

x: I–IV are correct: the PM advises the President on appointing Ministers, summoning and proroguing Parliament, dissolving the Lok Sabha and (through the Cabinet) Emergency. V is wrong: the CJI is appointed through the collegium process, not on the PM's advice.
t: Spot the appointment outside the PM's advice.

x: Both are true: Jawaharlal Nehru was India's first Prime Minister and also its longest-serving (1947–64).
t: Recall Nehru's two records.

x: Indira Gandhi was the first woman PM and Morarji Desai the first non-Congress PM. Charan Singh resigned in 1979 without ever facing the Lok Sabha, and Manmohan Singh sat in the Rajya Sabha throughout his tenure. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Match each 'first' to the right PM.
s: Match List-I with List-II: List-I a. Indira Gandhi b. Morarji Desai c. Charan Singh d. Manmohan Singh List-II i. First woman Prime Minister of India ii. First non-Congress Prime Minister of India iii. Prime Minister who never faced the Lok Sabha as Prime Minister iv. Prime Minister who was a Rajya Sabha member throughout his tenure Select the correct answer using the code given below:

x: C is incorrect: legally, Union Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President (Article 75(2)), though in practice he acts on the PM's advice.
t: Separate legal 'pleasure' from political practice.

x: The President administers the oath of office and the oath of secrecy to Union Ministers, in the forms given in the Third Schedule.
t: Recall who swears in Union Ministers.

x: A is true and B is false: Article 53 vests executive power in the President, who is the Head of State; the Prime Minister is Head of Government.
t: Head of State vs Head of Government.

x: The Prime Minister is Head of Government, other Ministers are appointed by the President on the PM's advice, the President is Head of State, and the Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Match each office to its role.
s: Match List-I with List-II: List-I (a) Prime Minister (b) Other Union Ministers (c) President (d) Vice-President List-II (i) Head of State (ii) Appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister (iii) Head of Government (iv) Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

x: A non-member can be a Minister for up to six consecutive months; he must enter either House in that time or cease to be a Minister.
t: Recall the six-month window.

x: C is incorrect: a Minister can speak in both Houses and joint sittings (Article 88), but can vote only in the House he belongs to.
t: Separate the right to speak from the right to vote.

x: Council of Ministers – about 60–80 members including PM, Cabinet Ministers, MoS and Deputy Ministers; Union Cabinet – about 15–20, the PM and Cabinet-rank Ministers only.
t: Separate the wide Council from the inner Cabinet.

x: The word 'Cabinet' was absent from the original Constitution and was inserted into Article 352(3) by the 44th Amendment (1978), requiring the Cabinet's written advice for an Emergency.
t: Link 'Cabinet' to the 44th Amendment.

x: D is incorrect: collective responsibility is owed only to the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha. Losing the Lok Sabha majority forces the whole Council to resign; individual Ministers answer for their portfolios.
t: Check which House holds the government accountable.

x: Article 75(1A), from the 91st Amendment (2003), limits Union Ministers, including the PM, to 15% of the Lok Sabha's total strength.
t: Recall the 15% ceiling.

x: Both are true: under Article 164(1A) a State ministry cannot exceed 15% of the Assembly's strength, and it must have at least 12 Ministers.
t: Remember both the ceiling and the floor of 12.

x: A is true, R is false: the PM's duty under Article 78 is real, but the PM is the Head of Government; the Head of State is the President.
t: Check the office named in R.

x: Under Article 78 the PM communicates all Council decisions and administrative proposals to the President, and puts an individual Minister's decision before the Council when the President requires.
t: Match each duty to its condition.

x: The Deputy Prime Minister is an extra-constitutional post created for political convenience; its holder has Cabinet rank but no powers above the PM.
t: Recall the post is not in the Constitution.

x: Two are correct: the Union Cabinet is the top tier of the ministerial hierarchy, and the Council of Ministers is a collective constitutional body. Statement 1 is wrong — the Cabinet, not the whole Council, is the core decision-making body. Statement 3 is wrong — the four tiers are a convention, not in the Constitution.
t: Separate the Cabinet's role from the Council's.

x: Patel's term as first Deputy PM (1947–1950), then the 44th Amendment (1978) and the 91st Amendment (2003): A, D, B, C.
t: Place both ends of Patel's tenure before the amendments.

x: The Union Council of Ministers is governed by Part V, Articles 74, 75, 77 and 78. Articles 163–167 in Part VI cover the State ministry.
t: Separate Union (Part V) from State (Part VI) Articles.

x: Both are true and R explains A: a Union Minister may sit in either House, so Lok Sabha membership is not required.
t: Ask whether R makes A follow.

x: Council of Ministers – the wider constitutional body; Cabinet – the compact inner core; the Council's composition – all categories of Ministers; the Cabinet's – PM and Cabinet-rank Ministers only.
t: Separate wide Council from inner Cabinet.

x: Both are true and R explains A: being a small inner group of senior Ministers is what lets the Cabinet act as the main decision-making body.
t: Ask whether size and seniority explain the role.

x: Article 75(2) – pleasure of the President; 75(3) – collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha; 75(5) – six months to become an MP; 88 – Ministers' right to speak in both Houses.
t: Match each clause to its rule.

x: C is incorrect: a confidence motion is moved by the government to prove its majority; a no-confidence motion is moved by the Opposition (Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha).
t: Remember who moves each motion.

x: A no-confidence motion is moved under Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha's Rules of Procedure. Articles 75(3) and 78 are constitutional provisions, not rules.
t: Link the no-confidence motion to Rule 198.

x: Three are correct: a Minister can take part in both Houses and joint sittings and must become an MP within six months. Statement 3 is wrong — he can vote only in his own House.
t: Separate speaking rights from voting rights.

x: Both are true: the Council of Ministers aids and advises the President (Article 74), and its powers rest on Articles 74 and 75.
t: Recall the Council's constitutional basis.
